trace.msg: Let's look at this puzzle carefully. I'll only move when I can explain why.
I can't rule out to (2,1,4), to (4,1,2) or to (2,2,1) yet, so I'll make an educated guess: to (2,1,4).

Contradiction! Every way forward fails: going to (2,2,1) would leave number 3 unreachable without crossing a higher number; going to (4,4,1) would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order); going to (6,2,1) would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order). So my guess (to (2,1,4) from number 1) was wrong. Next I'll try to (4,1,2).
I can't rule out to (4,1,4), to (6,1,2) or to (4,2,1) yet, so I'll make an educated guess: to (4,1,4).

Going to (4,1,6), the next 3 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (1,2,6); going to (6,1,4), the next 5 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (1,2,6). So the line goes to (2,1,4).
I can't rule out to (2,1,6) or to (1,2,4) yet, so I'll make an educated guess: to (2,1,6).

Going to (1,2,6), the next 4 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (6,1,6); going to (2,2,7), the next 3 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (6,1,6). So the line goes to (4,1,6).
Going to (4,2,7) would leave number 4 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes to (6,1,6).
Number 4 is only reachable this way.
The line must go to (7,4,6): to (7,2,4) is number 8, which comes later; to (6,2,7) is number 18, which comes later.
Going to (6,4,7) would force the line onto number 18 before its turn. So the line goes to (7,4,4).
The line must go to (7,6,4): to (7,2,4) is number 8, which comes later; to (7,4,2) is number 7, which comes later.
Going to (6,7,4) would leave number 6 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes to (7,6,2).
Number 6 is next and right here, so the line takes it.

Going to (4,4,1) would strand number 7: it would be left with only one free neighbour; going to (6,2,1) would strand number 7: it would be left with only one free neighbour. So the line goes to (7,4,2).
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (7,2,2).

Going to (6,1,2) would leave both cell (6,1,4) and cell (6,2,1) needing the line next, and it can't do both; going to (6,2,1) would strand number 8: it would be left with only one free neighbour. So the line goes to (7,2,4).
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (6,1,4).
Going to (4,4,1), the next move is forced and the line gets stuck at number 9. So the line goes to (2,2,1).
Number 9 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Cell (4,4,1) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (4,6,1).
Going to (4,7,2) would force the line onto number 12 before its turn. So the line goes to (2,6,1).
I can't rule out to (1,6,2) or to (2,7,2) yet, so I'll make an educated guess: to (1,6,2).
I can't rule out to (2,7,2) or to (1,6,4) yet, so I'll make an educated guess: to (2,7,2).
Going to (2,7,4), every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves. So the line goes to (4,7,2).
Number 12 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going to (6,7,6) would force the line onto number 16 before its turn. So the line goes to (4,7,4).
Going to (4,7,6), the next 8 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (4,6,7). So the line goes to (2,7,4).
Going to (2,7,6), the next move is forced and the line gets stuck at cell (1,6,6). So the line goes to (1,6,4).
The line must go to (1,6,6): to (1,4,4) is number 20, which comes later.
Number 14 is only reachable this way.
Going to (1,2,6) would cut off a group of 4 cells. So the line goes to (2,4,7).
Going to (2,2,7) would cut off a group of 5 cells. So the line goes to (2,6,7).
Cell (2,7,6) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (4,7,6).
Going to (4,6,7) leaves no safe move afterwards. So the line goes to (6,7,6).
Going to (6,6,7) would turn number 16 into a dead-end pocket with no way out. So the line goes to (7,6,6).
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (6,6,7).
Cell (4,6,7) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (4,4,7).
Cell (6,4,7) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (6,2,7).
Every cell is covered and the numbers are in order. Case closed!
I grow a search tree: my policy network suggests moves, a trained value head judge them. 56 simulations per move.
One of my simulated futures reached the end after 40 simulations. Following it!
Let evolution do the work: 24 random lines compete, the fittest breed and mutate.
Generation 0: the best random line covers 50/54 cells (93%).
Generation 2: fitness 54/54. The best line covers 54 cells.
Generation 2: a perfect line evolved! Every cell covered.
Feeling lucky! Before every move I'll play 24 random futures and bet on the move that survives most often.
Tried 72 futures: 67% survive going to (4,1,2) (best covers 67%); to (2,2,1) 58%; to (2,1,4) 50%.
Jackpot! A future after going to (4,1,4) covers the whole board. Cashing in!
Let x(cell, step) mean 'this cell is step number <step> of the line'. 54 cells x 54 steps, minus everything that's impossible at a glance.
Encoded 7,493 variables and 20,499 clauses in 0.10 s (2,198 position variables survive the pruning).
Solver found a model in 0.02 s. Decoding it into a line...
Q.E.D. Every clause is satisfied.
